Case study · GenAI prototype

Score Player

A blocky 3D arcade soccer game, taken from concept art to a playable prototype in one evening. I set the direction and made the art with GenAI image and 3D tools, then built the game by directing an AI coding agent.

Role
Creative direction, concept art, character design, game feel
Built
November 2026
Platform
Browser, phone and desktop (WebGL)
Play the prototype
Toolchain
ChatGPT · concept art, UI mockups Photoshop · paint-over, layout Meshy · 3D character model Claude · agentic coding of the game Three.js · real-time 3D in the browser Unreal Python · import pipeline
How it came together

From one frame to a playable match

01

Find the fun first

Before any art, I had a rough blocky 2v2 match built so I could feel the loop: dribble, charge a shot, beat the keeper. Once the core was fun, every later pass was about look and feel rather than rules.

02

Set the look with three frames

A cover, a gameplay frame and a profile screen defined the identity: purple dusk, gold crowns, chunky streetwear characters. The gameplay frame became the target for the camera, stadium and HUD.

03

Design the hero, then build him

I generated the character in 3D with Meshy, then produced a turnaround in his match kit: backwards purple cap with gold panels and a crown, neck headphones, flame jersey, "SHODE 10". The final Meshy model is in the game itself: converted to voxels with colours sampled from its texture, cut down from 400,000 triangles so it runs on a phone, and split into body, arms and legs so it can run and kick. The rest of the roster from my character sheet (Girl Gamer, Blonde Rival, Team Player, Skater and Pro Player) is built from that same model with voxel edits: new hair and headwear, hoodies, crop top, cargo pants and a backpack, each painted to its palette.

04

Rework the controls

The first touch layout had five floating action buttons. I moved to a retro console layout, a d-pad and four face buttons, and made it translucent so it never competes with the pitch.

05

Stadium, sound and voice

A two-tier bowl with an LED fascia, roof canopy, flags and corner floodlights, with the cover art on the big screen. Then audio: a chiptune loop, a crowd bed that swells on goals, a whistle, and spoken commentary with captions.

06

A pipeline for the next ten characters

To take this beyond one hero, I wrote Meshy to Unreal, a Python tool that batch-imports AI-generated characters into Unreal Engine 5 with correct naming, scale, texture settings and material instances, and lines them up in a level for review.

07

Package it as a product

A prototype answers "is it fun?". To show where it could go, I made the pitch around it: key art, feature panels for characters, customisation, stadiums, multiplayer and seasonal events, and a landing page that sells the game in one scroll. Every piece reuses the same crown, palette and cast, so the brand holds together from the store page to the pitch.

Concept pitch made for this portfolio. Score Player is not a Netflix release.

Creative calls

What I changed, and why

Controls

Swapped five floating buttons for a translucent d-pad and face-button layout.

The pitch is the product. Controls should read instantly and stay out of the way.

Camera

Moved from a high broadcast view to a low camera behind the player.

It sells the size of the stadium and keeps the goal and big screen ahead of you when you attack.

Character

Pushed proportions chunkier, with a bigger head and bold kit shapes.

On a phone, a player is a few hundred pixels tall. Silhouette and colour have to carry identity.

Identity

Repeated one crown motif across cap, banners, LED boards and scoreboard.

One symbol, used everywhere, makes a small game feel like a brand.

Next

Where I'd take it

  • Rig the Meshy model and bring the real asset into the game, with run, kick and celebration animations.
  • Replace the synthesized audio with a directed soundtrack and recorded or generated commentary in the game's voice.
  • Test with players to tune the shot assist, stamina and difficulty, and decide what the profile and progression screens should reward.
  • Prototype the features from the pitch, starting with kit customisation and a second themed stadium, to test which ones actually add fun.
